radiusSource: Choudhury et al. (2024), ApJL 971, L20, Table A.1: equatorial radius 11.36 +0.95/-0.63 km (68% credible interval) from NICER pulse-profile modelling (https://arxiv.org/abs/2407.06789): 11.36 +/- 0.95 km, inferred from the pulse shape.
massSource: Reardon et al. (2024), ApJL 971, L18, Table 1, PPTA-DR3: pulsar mass from the Shapiro delay (https://arxiv.org/abs/2407.07132)
distanceSource: 156.98 +/- 0.15 pc from Reardon et al. (2024), ApJL 971, L18, Table 1, PPTA-DR3: distance from the Shklovskii effect on the orbital period (https://arxiv.org/abs/2407.07132).
spinSource: Reardon et al. (2024), ApJL 971, L18, Table 1, PPTA-DR3: spin frequency, and the orbital inclination 137.506(16) degrees that Choudhury et al. (2024) use as the spin axis's inclination (https://arxiv.org/abs/2407.07132)
angularDiameterSource: Computed here from the radius and distance: 2 x 11.36 km at 156.98 pc. No telescope resolves it.

shape.qualification: A sphere at the radius the pulse-profile fit infers. The star spins fast enough to be slightly flattened, and gravity bends its light so that more than half the surface is visible at once; neither is drawn.
